meta.title: The Book That Reads You
meta.subtitle: An ergodic novel
meta.author: Xavier Phillipe
meta.description: You are not reading this book. It is reading you — in the margins.

sections.title: How to Read This Book
sections.subtitle: Please disobey
sections.content:
This is not a book you read straight through. It is a book you use. The story below is true. The notes in the margins are also true. They disagree. That is the point.

## The margin is a character

Two readers, M. and J., wrote in this copy before you. M. believes the narrator. J. does not. Follow their argument across Chapter One and the last chapter.

## Turn the book

Chapter Two must be read sideways, then upside down. A corridor does not run left to right.

## Trust no document

The Exhibits are a transcript, a checkout card and a memo. One of them is lying. The black bars are part of the story.

## The insert is loose

The Loose Insert reproduces a letter that was tucked inside this copy. In a real book it would fall out. Here it cannot — which is itself a clue.

## Choose, then live with it

Chapter Nine offers two endings. You may only believe one. The book will notice.

> “If a footnote tells you to stop reading, keep reading. If a margin tells you to turn back, you have already turned back.”
> — Ed., in the publisher’s hand

Start at Chapter One. Or start at the end and work backwards. The house does not mind. It has already seen you do both.

sections.title: The Copy
sections.content:
I found the book on the third floor of the library, in the aisle nobody dusts. It had no call number. It had my name in it, on page 47, in a hand I did not recognise and yet had practised for years.

“The girl will come back for this book,” the first line said. “She always does.”

::: margin M.
She says she did NOT take it home. But look at the Exhibits. The checkout card says she did. Who is lying — her, or the card?
:::

I told myself it was a coincidence. Names repeat. Libraries are full of coincidences that have been shelved in the wrong place. But the second line knew about the key I keep under the blue pot, and the third line knew I would lie about it.[^1]

::: margin M.
Also: page 47? This book is not that long. Count them. I did. Twice.
:::

I did not take the book home. I took it to the reading room and read it there, under the light that buzzes, until the librarian said, “We are closing,” in the voice people use for funerals.

[^1]: From the narrator: Dear margin, I can hear you writing. Stop underlining my lies. They are load-bearing.

sections.title: The Margin Replies
sections.content:
She reads on. The house in the book has one more room than the house she lives in. Every night she counts the rooms. Every night she gets a different number.

“Do not count the rooms,” the book says. “Count the doors that were not there yesterday.”

::: margin J.
M., you are being kind to her. She is NOT a reliable narrator. She counted the rooms wrong on purpose. Look — she says “third floor” in Chapter One, but this library (see the memo) has only two floors.
:::

::: margin M.
Then where did she find it, J.? If there is no third floor, there is no book, and if there is no book, who wrote THIS note? Checkmate. — M.
:::

::: margin J.
“The third floor is the one she built by reading. That is what ergodic means. You have to WORK to get there. Turn the page sideways. Go on. I dare you.”
:::

::: center
*→ The next chapter is sideways on purpose. →*
:::

sections.title: Turn the Book Sideways
sections.content:
::: center
*Turn the book 90° clockwise to read the corridor.*
:::

::: sideways
The corridor was longer on the way back.

That is the first rule of the house.

The second rule is: do not run.

Running makes the corridor longer.
:::

::: verse
I went down.
  One step.
    Another step.
      Another.
        The stairs
          did not end.
            They
              folded.
:::

::: center
There is no OUT in this diagram.

That is also a clue.
:::

::: upside-down
If you are reading this upside down, you have reached the bottom of the house. Congratulations. Do not look up.
:::

sections.title: Exhibits
sections.subtitle: From the file
sections.content:
## Exhibit A: Transcript

::: transcript
LIBRARIAN: Did you take the book home?
GIRL: No.
LIBRARIAN: The card says you did.
GIRL: Then the card is also reading the book.
[pause — 14 seconds, tape hiss]
LIBRARIAN: Please do not say that in here.
:::

## Exhibit B: Library checkout card

::: log
TITLE: The Book That Reads You
AUTHOR: ||Withheld by the house||
BORROWER: __________________
DATE DUE: NEVER
RETURNED: NO
NOTES: "Borrower claims book followed her home."
:::

## Exhibit C: Memo, with redactions

To: All staff. Re: the third floor. There is no third floor. Staff are reminded not to discuss the third floor, its ||corridor||, or the reader who ||left|| there on Tuesday. Thank you.

::: margin M.
One of these three documents is lying. I have boxed it. I will not tell you which. That would ruin the book. — M.
:::

sections.title: Loose Insert
sections.subtitle: Found tucked in this copy
sections.content:
*This page reproduces a loose insert. In print it would fall out.*

::: insert
Dear you,

If you found this letter, you are
already past the corridor, which means
you did not stop at Chapter Two.
Good. Most people stop.

Do not trust the footnotes in Chapter Nine.
They were written by the house.

— J. (the other reader,
not the one you think)
:::

::: margin M.
POSTSCRIPT, IN RED: J. is lying about the footnotes. — M.
:::

Editor’s note, printed below the insert: The letter is undated. The handwriting matches neither M. nor J. in our files. It matches yours. We checked. Please do not write back.

sections.title: House Log
sections.subtitle: Dossier • multi-voice file
sections.content:
::: log dark
[02:14] SYSTEM: Reader entered Chapter Eight.
[02:14] NARRATOR: I did not enter anything. I was already here.
[02:15] MARGIN_M: She says that every chapter. Note the pattern.
[02:15] SYSTEM: Warning: margin is now writing in the main text.
[02:16] MARGIN_J: Good. The main text was lying anyway.
[02:17] NARRATOR: I can see you both. Stop typing in my chapter.
[02:18] SYSTEM: ERROR: narrator and margin cannot be separated.
[02:19] READER (you): ...
[02:19] SYSTEM: Reader input recorded. Reader input will be used in Chapter Ten.
:::

**File note — for the reader:** This chapter borrows the dossier and chat-log shape: the story is not told, it is assembled from logs, messages and redactions. You, the reader, are the investigator. Assemble carefully.

sections.title: Choose
sections.content:
She reaches the last door. Behind it is either the way out, or another copy of this book.[^1][^2][^3][^4]

## Blackout poem — found in the margin, words left unredacted

::: center
||The reader|| you are already inside the book.
:::

*Read only the words that are NOT blacked out. That is the poem. That is also the warning.*

**Your choice, reader:**

☐ Believe the narrator

☐ Believe the margin

☐ Believe neither — and keep reading anyway

[^1]: If you believe the narrator, turn to Chapter Ten.

[^2]: A footnote to note 1: the narrator wrote note 1. Do not trust it.

[^3]: Note 2 was written by J. Do not trust J. either.

[^4]: If you believe the margin, turn back to Chapter One and start again. You have done this before. You will do it again.

sections.title: Or, The End (?)
sections.content:
She opens the last door. Behind it is a reading room. In the reading room is a girl, reading a book. The girl looks up. The girl is —

*[This sentence was removed by the reader.]*

::: margin M.
I told you not to trust the narrator. She never left the library. Neither did you. Neither did I. We are all still in Chapter One, really.
:::

::: margin J.
Speak for yourself, M. I left. I am writing this from outside the book. If you can read this, so are you.
:::
